config.title: Build product listing with sort filter search

intro.title: Build product listing with sort filter search
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build an interactive product listing page that allows users to view, sort, filter, and search through a set of products. You will learn how to manage and manipulate data using JavaScript arrays and objects. The main technologies involved include JavaScript functions, array methods like filter() and sort(), and event handling for user interactions. By the end, you'll have a functional web application that dynamically updates based on user input.
intro.usecase: This pattern is essential for any e-commerce platform, marketplace, or content-heavy application where users need to browse large datasets. For example, on Amazon or eBay, product listings feature sort options (by price, rating), filters (by category, brand), and a search bar to quickly find items. As a developer, you'll implement this to create intuitive user interfaces that help customers efficiently navigate and discover products, directly impacting user experience and conversion rates.

objectives: Construct a product data array with properties for filtering and sorting
Implement search functionality that filters products based on user input
Configure sort controls to manipulate product order by price or name
Initialize and update UI state to reflect filtered and sorted results
Bind event handlers to search and sort interface elements
Render dynamic product listings that respond to user interactions
Integrate search, filter, and sort features into a cohesive product display

steps.title: Create main ProductList component
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named ProductList that returns null for now.
steps.hint: Define a function called ProductList that returns null. You can use either a function declaration or arrow function syntax.
steps.expectedOutcome: A ProductList component function is defined and returns null.
successCriteria: The component is named ProductList and returns null.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure your component is named exactly 'ProductList' and returns null.
steps.feedbackWrong: That doesn't match what we need. Create a function called ProductList that returns null.

steps.title: Initialize product data array
steps.instruction: Inside your ProductList component, define a products array with at least 3 product objects. Each object should have id, name, price, and category properties.
steps.hint: Create an array of objects with consistent property names. Use numeric IDs, string names, numeric prices, and string categories.
steps.expectedOutcome: A products array is defined inside the component with at least 3 product objects, each containing id, name, price, and category.
successCriteria: products array exists with at least 3 objects, each object has id, name, price, and category properties
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You have an array, but check that each object has id, name, price, and category properties.
steps.feedbackWrong: The products array is missing or doesn't have the required structure. Make sure to define an array of objects with id, name, price, and category properties.

steps.title: Initialize state for filtered products
steps.instruction: Inside your ProductList component, call useState with the initial products array to create a state variable for filtered products. Destructure it as filteredProducts and setFilteredProducts.
steps.hint: Use the useState hook with the products array as the initial value. The first element of the returned array will hold the current filtered products, and the second will be the setter function.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: useState with an array
const [items, setItems] = useState([{ id: 1, name: 'Item 1' }]);
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a filteredProducts state variable initialized with the products array, and a setFilteredProducts function to update it.
successCriteria: The useState hook is called with the products array, and the destructured variables are named filteredProducts and setFilteredProducts.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're calling useState with the products array and destructuring the result as filteredProducts and setFilteredProducts.
steps.feedbackWrong: That doesn't match the expected implementation. Review how to use useState with an array initial value.

steps.title: Initialize state for sort option
steps.instruction: Initialize a state variable for the sort option with an initial value of 'name'.
steps.hint: Use the useState hook to create a state variable and its setter function. The initial value should be the string 'name'.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: state for a selected option
const [selectedOption, setSelectedOption] = useState('default');
steps.expectedOutcome: A state variable named sortOption and a setter function named setSortOption are declared with an initial value of 'name'.
successCriteria: The useState hook is called with 'name' as the initial value, and the returned array is destructured into sortOption and setSortOption.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're using useState with 'name' as the initial value and destructuring the result into sortOption and setSortOption.
steps.feedbackWrong: The state for the sort option isn't set up correctly. Use useState with 'name' as the initial value.

steps.title: Define handleSort function
steps.instruction: Define a function named handleSort inside your component that takes an event parameter and sorts the filteredProducts array based on the selected sort option.
steps.hint: Create a function that updates the sortOption state and sorts the filteredProducts array. You can use a switch statement or if/else to handle different sort options.
steps.expectedOutcome: A handleSort function is defined inside the ProductList component that will handle sorting logic when called.
successCriteria: The handleSort function is defined with an event parameter and contains logic to update sortOption and sort filteredProducts.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've started defining the function, but make sure it takes an event parameter and includes logic for sorting.
steps.feedbackWrong: The handleSort function is not properly defined. Check that you've created a function named handleSort inside the component.

steps.title: Add container div and search input
steps.instruction: In your component's return statement, replace the current null with a container div that contains a search input element. The input should have type='text', placeholder='Search products...', value bound to your searchQuery state, and onChange wired to your handleSearch function.
steps.hint: Remember to use JSX syntax for the div and input elements. The input's value should be your searchQuery state variable, and onChange should call handleSearch with the event.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component now returns a container div with a search input element that has proper value binding and event handling.
successCriteria: The return statement contains a div with an input element that has type='text', placeholder='Search products...', value={searchQuery}, and onChange={handleSearch}.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that your input has all required attributes: type='text', placeholder, value bound to searchQuery, and onChange wired to handleSearch.
steps.feedbackWrong: The search input structure isn't quite right. Make sure you're returning a div with an input element that has the correct attributes and event handler.

steps.title: Add sort select dropdown
steps.instruction: Inside the return statement of your ProductList component, add a <select> element with an onChange handler that calls handleSort and a value attribute bound to sortOption. Include two <option> elements inside: one with value='name' and label 'Sort by Name', and another with value='price' and label 'Sort by Price'.
steps.hint: Place the <select> element after the search input. Remember to set onChange={handleSort} and value={sortOption}.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: a dropdown for selecting a category
<select value={category} onChange={handleCategoryChange}>
  <option value="electronics">Electronics</option>
  <option value="clothing">Clothing</option>
</select>
steps.expectedOutcome: A dropdown menu appears below the search input, allowing users to choose between sorting by name or price. The dropdown's value is controlled by the sortOption state, and changing it triggers the handleSort function.
successCriteria: The return statement includes a <select> element with onChange={handleSort} and value={sortOption}, containing two <option> elements with values 'name' and 'price'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added a dropdown, but check that it has both onChange={handleSort} and value={sortOption}, and includes both 'name' and 'price' options.
steps.feedbackWrong: The dropdown is missing or incomplete. Ensure you add a <select> element with onChange={handleSort}, value={sortOption}, and two <option> elements for 'name' and 'price'.
